newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain security official gloomy on peace with ETA.
newsitem.headline: Spain security official gloomy on peace with ETA.

text.p: Spain's top strategist in the battle against Basque separatists was pessimistic about the chances of peace after a week of deadly attacks and predicted Secretary of State for Security Ricardo Marti Fluxa said in a newspaper interview on Sunday that France's pursuit of ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) separatist rebels meant the group would likely seek alternative bases of operation.
"It is a difficult moment to send out a message of optimism," Fluxa told the newspaper El Pais.
The government has blamed ETA for three deadly attacks in the past week, one of them the assassination of a Supreme Court judge in Madrid.
Fluxa, number two at the Interior Ministry, is directly responsible for dealing with violent Basque groups.
"ETA is suffering from a degeneration...in a process which could last for a long time and cause us much pain," he said.
It would be easier to fight ETA if the group's leadership were in Spain rather than France, Fluxa said.
"The ideal situation for ETA is to have its leadership in France and the operative commandos in Spain."
He praised France's tougher stance against ETA.
"At this moment, they are pursued identically in Spain and France," he said. "With the persecution they suffer in France, what they will do is move to other places," he predicted.
Fluxa said it was unlikely ETA would launch attacks on French targets and if they did, he predicted they would be "sporadic and targeted".

The recent wave of violence has only hardened the government's refusal to negotiate with ETA until they lay down their arms and release two hostages. "(ETA) will never achieve negotiations by putting dead people on the table," Fluxa said.
On ETA's strength, he said the group has six or seven commandos (groups) who gather intelligence and "very few" operatives, whose numbers he put at between six and 12 people.
"It is absolutely senseless to think six or eight individuals could crush the state. We will use all the means the Constitution grants us to overcome them."
Asked about ETA's financial situation, he replied "I don't think it's bad. They have many ways of getting financing."
The government hopes to chip away at the organisation's financial structure, Fluxa said, but he acknowledged it was difficult.
